Gori Jewish Section on municipal cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Gori, Georgia

Not demolished. Gori, one of Georgia's oldest cities and regional capital of Shida Kartli, had scattered Jewish presence possibly as early as the 1670s (per French traveler Jean Chardin's account of Gori as a trading hub), with settlement more firmly established by the early 19th century. An 1831 Russian survey counted 504 Jewish men in the wider Gori district; by 1897, city Jewish population stood at 64. Jews and Armenians dominated Gori's domestic trade. Around 40 Jewish families lived in Gori by the early 20th century, worshipping in a shared two-story building with a synagogue on the top floor and a communal bath below. After Soviet religious suppression in 1936 destroyed the original building, the community bought a new private house for a synagogue, expanding it with a second floor in 1953, complete with a matzah oven and mikveh. The cemetery's oldest legible tombstone dates to 1939, though it remains active today, regularly cleaned with financial support from relatives of the deceased now living in Israel. Notably, Joseph Stalin was born in Gori, now home to a museum dedicated to him.
